name: Axolotl
range: Only the canals of Lake Xochimilco, at the southern edge of Mexico City
tagline: The salamander that never grows up
lede: Most salamanders trade their gills for lungs and leave the water. The axolotl never does. It spends its whole life looking like an oversized tadpole with a permanent smile, feathery gills fanning out from its head like a crown.
home: Wild axolotls live in just one place on Earth: the canals and wetlands of Xochimilco, a remnant of the great lake that once surrounded the Aztec capital. They need cool, clean, still water with plenty of plants to hide in.
anatomy: An axolotl's most striking features are the three pairs of feathery gills that sweep back from its head. Each stalk is fringed with fine filaments that are packed with blood vessels, which is why they often look pink or red; the more filaments, the more oxygen it can pull from the water. Its eyes are small and lidless, and its eyesight is poor, so it relies heavily on smell and on a lateral line, a row of pressure-sensitive cells along each side that feels the faint ripples made by moving prey. Wild axolotls are dark, mottled olive and brown with gold flecks, ideal for hiding on a muddy bed. The pale pink, golden and white axolotls in pet shops come from captive lines. Its teeth are tiny cones used to grip rather than chew, so prey is swallowed whole. Unusually, it carries a huge genome: about ten times more DNA than a human.
life: Axolotls hunt by ambush, waiting on the muddy bottom and then sucking in worms, insect larvae, small crustaceans and fish with a sudden gulp. They breathe through their gills, their skin, and simple lungs, swimming up now and then to gulp air.
family: Axolotls breed in the cool months, from roughly December to June. A courting male nudges the female and performs a sort of slow waggling dance, then deposits small packets of sperm on the lake bed. The female picks one up with her cloaca and later lays between a few hundred and around a thousand eggs, sticking them one by one to water plants and stones. The eggs hatch after about two weeks into tiny larvae that must start hunting almost immediately, first on microscopic animals, then on larger prey as they grow. Neither parent looks after the young, and adults will eat eggs and larvae, including their own. Axolotls can breed when they are about a year old. In captivity, a single female may spawn several times a year, which is one reason the species is so common in laboratories even while it vanishes in the wild.
remarkable: Scientists call it neoteny: the axolotl keeps its juvenile features for life and still breeds. Even stranger, it can regrow lost limbs, its tail, parts of its spinal cord and even parts of its heart and brain, without scarring. Labs around the world study it to learn how.
outlook: Millions of axolotls live in aquariums and labs, but in the wild they are critically endangered. Pollution, the spread of Mexico City, and introduced carp and tilapia that eat their eggs have pushed the wild population to the edge. Local farmers are restoring traditional chinampa canals as refuges.
people: The Aztecs ate axolotls and featured them in their stories, and for centuries they were sold in Mexico City markets as food and medicine. European scientists first saw living axolotls in 1864, when a batch was sent to Paris. To everyone's astonishment, a few of them later transformed into land-dwelling salamanders, revealing that the axolotl could change but normally doesn't. Since then it has become one of the most studied amphibians in the world, used in research on regeneration, embryos and cancer. In modern Mexico it is a cultural icon: it appears on the 50-peso banknote, in murals, festivals and toys, and has a museum devoted to it in Chapultepec Park. Scientists from the National Autonomous University of Mexico work with local farmers in Xochimilco to keep canals clean and create refuges, and visitors can 'adopt' an axolotl to fund the work.
didYouKnow: The name comes from Nahuatl and is often linked to Xolotl, the Aztec god of fire and lightning, who was said to have transformed into an axolotl to escape death.

name: Monarch Butterfly
range: Across North America in summer; eastern monarchs winter in the mountains of central Mexico
tagline: A featherweight that crosses a continent
lede: Each autumn, monarchs from southern Canada and the eastern United States fly up to 4,500 kilometres to a few mountain forests in Mexico. None of them has ever been there before. Their great-grandparents left the previous spring.
home: In summer, monarchs spread across meadows, roadsides and gardens wherever milkweed grows, from the Maritimes to the Prairies. In winter, the eastern population packs into oyamel fir forests high in central Mexico, millions of butterflies hanging from single trees like orange leaves.
anatomy: Like all butterflies, a monarch has four wings covered in thousands of tiny overlapping scales, which create its orange and black pattern. You can tell males from females by looking at the hind wings: males have a small black spot on a vein of each hind wing, made of special scent scales, and slightly thinner black veins. Monarchs taste with their feet, which helps a female check that a leaf is milkweed before laying an egg on it. Adults feed through a long, coiled tube called a proboscis that unrolls to sip nectar. Their compound eyes can see ultraviolet light, and the clock genes in their antennae are essential to navigation: in experiments, monarchs with painted-over antennae lose their sense of direction. The striped caterpillar has two pairs of black tentacles, one at each end, which it uses to feel its way and may help confuse predators.
life: A monarch caterpillar eats only milkweed. Over about two weeks it grows roughly two thousand times heavier, then hangs upside down and forms a jade-green chrysalis studded with gold dots. Summer adults live just a few weeks, but the autumn generation can live for eight months.
family: A female monarch lays each egg singly, usually on the underside of a young milkweed leaf, and may lay several hundred over her short life. The egg hatches in three to five days. The caterpillar's first meal is its own eggshell, then it starts on the milkweed, carefully chewing a circle to drain the leaf's sticky latex before eating. It sheds its skin four times as it grows. After about two weeks, it hangs head-down in a J shape and forms its chrysalis, which turns from jade green to see-through just before the adult emerges, roughly ten to fourteen days later. Summer butterflies mate and lay eggs within days. The autumn generation is different: shorter days and cooler temperatures switch off breeding, so these butterflies put all their energy into migrating and surviving the winter, mating only when spring arrives.
remarkable: Milkweed contains toxins that monarchs store in their bodies, making them taste terrible to birds. Their bright orange wings are a warning sign. On migration they navigate using a sun compass in their antennae and brain that corrects for the time of day.
outlook: Monarch numbers have fallen sharply over recent decades. Milkweed has been lost to herbicides and development, the Mexican forests face logging, and extreme weather hits the migration. Planting native milkweed and nectar flowers is one of the most direct ways anyone can help.
people: For centuries, people in central Mexico knew that millions of butterflies appeared each November, around the Day of the Dead, and many saw them as the returning souls of ancestors. Scientists didn't know where North America's monarchs went until 1975, when a team following decades of tagging work by Canadian zoologist Fred Urquhart found the overwintering forests in the mountains west of Mexico City. Today part of that area is protected as the Monarch Butterfly Biosphere Reserve, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and tourism provides local communities with income. Citizen scientists across Canada and the United States tag monarchs with tiny stickers, count them at milkweed patches, and plant 'waystations' of milkweed and nectar flowers in gardens and schoolyards. The monarch is also the official insect or butterfly of several US states, and a symbol of the three countries working together to protect it.
didYouKnow: It takes three to four generations of monarchs, each living only weeks, to travel north again in spring. Then a single long-lived generation makes the whole trip south.

name: Rusty Patched Bumble Bee
range: Once from southern Ontario and Quebec to Georgia; now scattered patches of the US Midwest and Northeast
tagline: A common bee that quietly vanished
lede: Twenty-five years ago, this fuzzy bee buzzed through gardens and meadows from southern Ontario to the Carolinas. Then, within a decade, it disappeared from most of its range. In 2017 it became the first bumble bee protected under the US Endangered Species Act.
home: Rusty patched bumble bees need open grasslands, prairies and woodland edges with flowers blooming from early spring to autumn, plus undisturbed ground for nests and winter shelter. In Canada it was last confirmed in 2009, at Pinery Provincial Park in Ontario.
anatomy: Rusty patched bumble bees are round, fuzzy bees with mostly yellow and black bands. Queens are larger than workers and lack the rusty patch, which is why identification needs a close look. Their dense hair keeps them warm and collects pollen, which they comb into pollen baskets on their hind legs, flat shiny areas fringed with stiff hairs. Like other bumble bees, they have a fairly long tongue for reaching nectar deep inside flowers. Females have a smooth stinger they can use more than once, but bumble bees are gentle and sting only when handled or when their nest is threatened. They see ultraviolet light and patterns on petals that are invisible to us, and they can even sense the weak electric charge of a flower, which changes briefly after another bee has visited, helping them skip flowers that have just been emptied.
life: Each colony lasts a single year. A queen wakes in spring, finds an old rodent burrow, and raises the first workers alone. By late summer the colony may hold hundreds of bees. Then new queens mate, dig into the soil, and are the only ones to survive the winter.
family: Each spring, a mated queen emerges from her winter hideaway in loose soil and searches for a nest site, often an abandoned rodent burrow. She builds a wax pot of nectar and a small mound of pollen, lays her first eggs on it, and keeps them warm by shivering her flight muscles and pressing her body against the brood, much like a bird on its nest. These first daughters become workers, taking over foraging while the queen stays home to lay eggs. Rusty patched colonies grow large for bumble bees and remain active into autumn. Late in the season, the colony switches to raising males and new queens. They leave to mate, the old queen and her workers die as the weather cools, and only the young queens dig in for the winter, carrying the next year's colonies inside them.
remarkable: Bumble bees can 'buzz pollinate': they grip a flower and vibrate their flight muscles so fast that pollen shakes loose. Tomatoes, blueberries and cranberries are pollinated best this way. Workers wear a small rusty-orange patch on their abdomen, which gives the species its name.
outlook: The species has lost around ninety percent of its population. Habitat loss, pesticides such as neonicotinoids, diseases spread from managed bees, and a warming climate all play a part. Leaving lawns a little wild, planting early and late bloomers and skipping pesticides gives native bees a chance.
people: The rusty patched bumble bee was once so common that few people noticed it. Its collapse was spotted in the late 1990s by researchers studying bumble bees in the US Midwest, and in 2017 it became the first bumble bee, and the first bee in the continental United States, to be listed as endangered. In Canada it is listed as Endangered under the Species at Risk Act, and surveys continue in southern Ontario in the hope that it still survives there. Much of what we know about its current range comes from volunteers: projects such as Bumble Bee Watch ask people to photograph bumble bees and upload them so experts can identify them. Gardeners can help by planting native flowers like wild bergamot, goldenrod and asters, leaving some leaf litter and bare ground, and avoiding pesticides.
didYouKnow: Bumble bees can fly in cooler weather than most bees because they shiver their flight muscles to warm up before take-off.

name: Luna Moth
range: Deciduous forests of eastern North America, from Nova Scotia and southern Ontario to Florida and Texas
tagline: A ghost-green moth that lives for a week
lede: On a warm night in early summer, something the size of a hand drifts past the porch light: pale green wings, long trailing tails, and two eyespots. The luna moth is one of the largest and loveliest moths in North America, and it has only days to live.
home: Luna moths live in hardwood forests across eastern North America. In Canada they occur from Saskatchewan to Nova Scotia, where there is one generation each summer. Farther south, two or three generations hatch each year.
anatomy: Luna moths belong to the giant silk moths, a family of big, heavy-bodied moths. Their wings are a soft lime green, edged with a band of purple or brown in the north and yellow in the south, and each wing carries a transparent eyespot that may startle predators. The long hind-wing tails twist as the moth flies. Males have very broad, feathery antennae covered in sensors that can detect a few molecules of a female's scent; females have narrower antennae. Adults have no working mouth and a reduced digestive system, since they never feed. The caterpillar is bright green with small red or yellow bumps, and grows to about 7 centimetres. When threatened it rears up, clicks its jaws and may regurgitate a bitter fluid. Its colour matches the leaves it eats so well that most people never notice one.
life: Caterpillars spend weeks munching the leaves of birch, walnut, hickory, sweetgum and persimmon, then spin a papery cocoon wrapped in leaves. The adult that emerges has no working mouth. It never eats, living on stored energy for about a week, just long enough to find a mate.
family: Female luna moths release their scent, called a pheromone, after dark, usually around midnight, and males fly in from far away. They mate through the early morning. The next evening the female begins laying around 200 to 300 eggs, in small groups on the leaves of the trees her caterpillars will eat. The eggs hatch after about a week. The caterpillars molt five times over several weeks, eating heavily. When fully grown, a caterpillar spins a thin silk cocoon wrapped in leaves, which usually falls to the forest floor. In Canada, the luna moth spends the winter as a pupa inside this cocoon, hidden in the leaf litter, and the adult emerges in late spring or early summer. Further south, summer generations follow one another quickly, and the last of the year overwinters the same way.
remarkable: Those long hindwing tails are a defense against bats. As the moth flies, the twisting tails scatter the bat's sonar echoes, so the bat strikes the tail instead of the body. Males can smell a female's scent from a great distance with their broad, feathery antennae.
outlook: Luna moths are still widespread, but like many night insects they are affected by pesticides, habitat loss and artificial light, which draws them away from mating and into the paths of predators. Turning off outdoor lights on summer nights is a simple way to help.
people: The luna moth was named in the 1700s after the Roman moon goddess Luna, for its pale colour and night flights. It has become one of the most recognisable moths in North America and a favourite of photographers and nature lovers, appearing on a 1987 US postage stamp. Because the adults are so short-lived and only active at night, seeing one is often a memorable event. Like many night-flying insects, luna moths are drawn to artificial light, where they waste precious time and energy and are easier for birds and bats to catch. Many conservation groups now recommend turning off unnecessary outdoor lights or using warm, shielded bulbs. Keeping native trees such as birch, walnut and hickory, and leaving fallen leaves under them over the winter, protects the cocoons that are resting there until spring.
didYouKnow: A luna caterpillar can make a clicking sound with its mandibles and spit a bitter fluid when it is disturbed.

quiz.prompt: Why doesn't an adult luna moth eat?
choices: It eats only once, on its first night
It shares food from its caterpillar siblings
quiz.explanation: Adult luna moths have no functional mouthparts and live on energy stored as caterpillars.

quiz.prompt: What do the long tails on its wings do?
quiz.explanation: The spinning tails scatter bat echolocation, so bats aim for the tails instead of the body.

quiz.prompt: How long does an adult luna moth live?
quiz.explanation: With no way to eat, the adult lives for roughly seven to ten days.

name: Common Loon
range: Breeds on lakes across Canada and the northern US; winters on Atlantic and Pacific coasts
tagline: The voice of the northern lake
lede: If you've heard a wild, echoing wail across a dark lake, you've heard a loon. Few sounds say 'northern wilderness' more clearly. The common loon is so woven into Canadian life that it appears on the one-dollar coin, which everyone calls the 'loonie'.
home: In summer, loons nest on clear, quiet lakes from Newfoundland to Alaska, usually one pair per small lake. They need clean water and plenty of fish. In winter they move to ice-free ocean coasts, trading their checkerboard breeding plumage for plain grey.
anatomy: The common loon has a long, dagger-shaped bill, a black head with a glossy green sheen in summer, a striped white necklace, and a black-and-white checkerboard back. Its eyes are a deep red, which may help it see underwater, where red light fades quickly. Loons have special muscles that change the shape of their lenses, so they can focus both in air and underwater. Their bones are solid rather than hollow, and they can squeeze air out of their feathers and lungs to sink quietly. Their legs sit so far back that they cannot easily walk, but they make loons powerful underwater swimmers that chase fish with their feet. Their wings are small for their weight, which is why they need a long run across the water to take off. In the air, though, loons are fast fliers, reaching speeds of over 100 km/h.
life: Loons are built for diving. Unlike most birds, their bones are solid rather than hollow, so they can sink easily, and they can dive to around 60 metres while chasing fish. Chicks ride on their parents' backs for their first weeks, staying warm and safe from pike and snapping turtles.
family: Loons usually pair up with the same partner for several years and return to the same lake. They build a simple nest of plants right at the water's edge, because they can barely walk, and lay one or two olive-brown eggs. Both parents take turns incubating for about four weeks. Chicks can swim almost immediately but ride on their parents' backs for the first couple of weeks to rest and stay warm. Both parents feed them small fish and insects, and the chicks learn to dive and catch their own food over the summer. By around 11 or 12 weeks, the young can fly. In autumn the adults leave first, and the young follow later on their own. Young loons stay on the ocean for two or three years before returning north to breed.
remarkable: A loon's legs sit far back on its body, perfect for swimming but terrible for walking, so it barely shuffles on land. To take off, it runs across the water for a long runway. Its calls each mean something: the wail keeps in touch, the tremolo signals alarm, and only males yodel to defend territory.
outlook: Loons are widespread, but they are sensitive to lead fishing tackle, which they swallow with grit, to mercury and acid rain, and to boat wakes that swamp shoreline nests. Lead-free tackle and giving nesting loons space help a lot.
people: Loons have long been important in Indigenous stories across North America. In some Anishinaabe traditions the loon is a clan animal, and its calls appear in many legends. To settlers and cottagers, the loon's wail came to symbolise the northern wilderness, and it appears on the Canadian one-dollar coin, introduced in 1987, which gave the coin its nickname 'loonie'. It is Ontario's provincial bird and Minnesota's state bird. Loons are sensitive indicators of lake health. Many are poisoned after swallowing lead sinkers or jigs, which they mistake for the pebbles they swallow to help digestion, so several provinces and states encourage or require lead-free tackle. Volunteers across Canada take part in loon surveys each summer, counting pairs and chicks to track how lakes are doing.
didYouKnow: The common loon is the provincial bird of Ontario and the state bird of Minnesota.

quiz.explanation: Legs placed far back are great for diving but make walking almost impossible.

quiz.explanation: Only males yodel, and they use it to defend their territory.

name: Atlantic Puffin
range: North Atlantic coasts: Newfoundland and Labrador, Maine, Iceland, Norway, the Faroes and Britain
tagline: The clown of the North Atlantic
lede: With its rainbow bill, orange feet and sad-clown eyes, the Atlantic puffin looks like a cartoon. But this little seabird is a tough ocean traveller that spends most of its life far out at sea, coming ashore only to raise a single chick.
home: Puffins nest in huge colonies on grassy clifftops and rocky islands across the North Atlantic. Iceland holds the largest share of the world's population, and Newfoundland's Witless Bay hosts North America's biggest colony. In winter they scatter across the open ocean.
anatomy: An Atlantic puffin is a small, chunky seabird with a black back, white belly and white face. In summer its large, triangular bill is striped with blue, yellow and bright orange, with a fleshy yellow rosette at the corners of the mouth. Small dark horn-like plates above and below its eyes give it a sad expression. Puffins' bills even glow under ultraviolet light, which other puffins may be able to see. Their wings are short and strong, built more for 'flying' underwater than in the air, so they must flap very fast to stay aloft. Underwater they use their wings to pursue fish and their orange feet to steer, and they can dive down to around 60 metres, although most dives are much shallower. Spines on the roof of the mouth and a rough tongue hold caught fish in place while the puffin keeps hunting.
life: Puffins dig burrows with their bills and feet and lay one egg. Both parents bring fish to the chick, called a puffling. Using a rough tongue and spines on the roof of their mouths, they can hold a row of small fish crosswise in their bills, often ten or more at once.
family: Puffins usually return to the same mate and the same burrow every year, greeting each other by tapping and rubbing their bills together, a display called billing. They dig their burrows up to about a metre long using their bills and feet, or take over rabbit holes, and line the nest chamber with grass and feathers. The female lays a single white egg, and both parents take turns incubating it for about six weeks. The chick, called a puffling, is fed small fish several times a day. After about six weeks in the dark burrow, the puffling leaves at night, flying or tumbling down to the sea, and swims away from land. It spends its first few years entirely at sea and returns to the colony when it is around three to five years old, first breeding at about five.
remarkable: Puffins 'fly' underwater with their wings, diving for sand eels, herring and capelin. In the air they flap up to 400 times a minute and can reach about 80 km/h. Their famous bill is only bright in the breeding season; in winter they shed its colorful outer plates.
outlook: Puffins are listed as vulnerable because European colonies have declined, linked to warming seas that move their prey, overfishing and storms. In Maine, the long-running Project Puffin brought puffins back to islands where they had vanished a century ago.
people: People in Iceland, the Faroe Islands and Norway have hunted puffins for food for centuries, using long-handled nets to catch birds in flight, and in some places limited hunting continues today. In the 1800s and early 1900s, hunting wiped out puffin colonies on many islands in the Gulf of Maine. In 1973, American biologist Stephen Kress started Project Puffin, bringing young puffins from Newfoundland to Eastern Egg Rock in Maine and using wooden decoys and mirrors to persuade returning birds the island was safe. It worked, and puffins now nest on several Maine islands again. The Atlantic puffin is Newfoundland and Labrador's provincial bird and a huge draw for tourism, from Witless Bay to Iceland's Westman Islands, where every summer local children rescue lost pufflings attracted to town lights.
didYouKnow: On some Icelandic islands, children rescue confused pufflings that land in town at night and release them toward the sea the next morning.

name: North American Beaver
range: Streams, ponds and lakes across almost all of Canada and the United States
tagline: Nature's master builder
lede: Few animals reshape the land like the beaver. With nothing but teeth, paws and determination, a family of beavers can turn a trickling stream into a pond, flood a forest, and create a wetland that hundreds of other species depend on.
home: Beavers live wherever there is slow water and trees: from Arctic river deltas to desert streams. They build dome-shaped lodges of sticks and mud with underwater entrances, so they can come and go unseen and stay safe from wolves and coyotes.
anatomy: The beaver is North America's largest rodent. Its thick brown fur has two layers: long, coarse guard hairs and a dense, soft underfur that traps air and keeps the skin dry. Beavers comb oil from glands near their tail through their fur with a split claw on each hind foot. Their big, webbed hind feet push them through the water, while the small, nimble front paws carry sticks, mud and food. The famous tail is flat, scaly and wide; it works as a rudder, a prop to lean on while gnawing, a fat store for winter, and an alarm, slapped hard on the water to warn the family of danger. Beavers can close their lips behind their front teeth, so they can gnaw underwater without swallowing water, and valves close their ears and nostrils when they dive.
life: Beavers are vegetarians. They eat bark, twigs, leaves and water plants, and in autumn they store a pile of branches underwater near the lodge to feed on through the winter, even when the pond is frozen. Families of parents and young stay together for about two years.
family: Beavers live in family groups, usually a breeding pair that stays together for many years, plus their young from this year and last year. Kits are born in late spring inside the lodge, typically two to four at a time. They have fur and open eyes at birth, and can swim within a day, though they cannot dive well at first because their fur is so buoyant. The whole family helps raise them: yearlings bring food and help repair the dam and lodge. Young beavers stay with their parents for about two years, learning to build, then leave to find their own territory, sometimes travelling many kilometres. Families mark their territory with mounds of mud scented with castoreum, a musky substance from glands near the tail, and keep strangers away.
remarkable: A beaver's front teeth never stop growing, and their orange color comes from iron in the enamel, which makes them extra tough. Clear inner eyelids act like goggles, valves seal their ears and nose, and they can stay underwater for about 15 minutes.
outlook: The fur trade nearly wiped beavers out by the 1800s. Today they have bounced back, and scientists now see them as allies: beaver ponds store water during droughts, slow floods, filter pollutants and create rich habitat for fish, birds and frogs.
people: The beaver shaped Canada's history. Beaver fur made a dense, waterproof felt prized for hats in Europe, and from the 1600s the fur trade drove exploration and settlement, founded companies like the Hudson's Bay Company, and changed the lives of many Indigenous peoples who trapped and traded furs. By the late 1800s beavers had been wiped out across much of the continent. Protection, reintroductions and the end of the fashion for beaver hats allowed them to return, and today there may be millions. Beavers can cause trouble, flooding roads and farmland, but many communities now use 'beaver deceivers', pipes that let water flow through a dam without the beavers noticing, so people and beavers can coexist. The beaver appears on the Canadian five-cent coin, and Parks Canada's logo features one.
didYouKnow: The beaver became an official national symbol of Canada in 1975.

name: Moose
range: Northern forests of Canada, Alaska, the northern US, Scandinavia and Siberia
tagline: The giant of the northern forest
lede: The moose is the largest deer that has ever lived in modern times, standing taller at the shoulder than most people. Despite their size and gangly legs, moose move silently through dense forest and are surprisingly graceful swimmers.
home: Moose live in the boreal forests that ring the top of the world, from Newfoundland to Alaska and across Scandinavia and Russia. They love places where forest meets water: lakes, bogs and marshes full of the plants they eat.
anatomy: A moose looks almost mismatched: long legs, a short neck, a humped back, and a long face with an overhanging, flexible upper lip that strips leaves from branches. That big nose is more than it seems; it contains a large, complex nasal cavity, and moose can close their nostrils when they put their heads underwater to feed. Under the chin hangs a flap of skin called a bell or dewlap, whose purpose is still debated. Their coat is made of long, hollow guard hairs over a woolly undercoat, excellent insulation in winter but a problem in summer heat, which is one reason moose spend so much time in water. Long legs let them step over fallen logs and walk through snow up to about 90 centimetres deep. A bull's broad, palm-shaped antlers can weigh over 30 kilograms and are grown in about five months each year.
life: Moose are browsers, eating leaves, twigs and bark from willow, birch and aspen. In summer they wade into ponds to eat water plants, even dunking their heads underwater. An adult can eat more than 30 kilograms of food a day in summer.
family: Moose mate in September and October, the season called the rut. Bulls stop eating much, call with deep grunts, thrash bushes with their antlers and sometimes fight rivals by locking antlers and shoving. Cows call with long, moaning wails. After about eight months, in late May or June, the cow gives birth to one calf, sometimes twins, in a sheltered spot, often near water. Calves are reddish-brown and can stand within a day. They grow fast on rich milk, gaining well over a kilogram a day, and can outrun a person within a few days. The mother is fiercely protective, and the calf stays with her for about a year, until she drives it away shortly before her next calf is born. Wolves and bears take many calves, so their first year is the most dangerous.
remarkable: A bull's antlers can span more than 1.8 metres and are among the fastest-growing tissues of any animal. They are shed every winter and regrown each spring. Moose can swim for kilometres, dive several metres, and their long legs carry them through deep snow.
outlook: Moose are common across most of their range, but in some southern areas they are declining. Warmer winters let winter ticks thrive, and thousands of ticks can weaken a single moose. A brain worm carried by deer is another growing threat.
people: The name 'moose' comes from an Algonquian word, often translated as 'twig eater' or 'he strips off'. For thousands of years moose have been a major source of meat, hide, sinew and bone for Indigenous peoples across the North, and hunting remains important in many communities today. Moose are hugely popular with wildlife watchers, and parks such as Algonquin in Ontario draw visitors hoping to see one by the road. They can also be dangerous: collisions between cars and moose are a serious hazard in Newfoundland, Scandinavia and elsewhere, and a frightened or protective moose can charge. Moose were introduced to Newfoundland in 1904, where only a handful were released, and there are now over 100,000. Wildlife biologists track moose health closely, studying the effects of ticks, parasites and warming winters.
didYouKnow: In Britain and much of Europe, this animal is called an 'elk'. In North America, 'elk' means a completely different deer, the wapiti.

quiz.prompt: What happens to a bull moose's antlers each winter?
choices: They fall off and regrow in spring
quiz.explanation: Moose shed their antlers every winter and grow a new set each year.

quiz.prompt: What is the moose called in Britain?
quiz.explanation: In British English the moose is called an elk, which confuses many North Americans.

quiz.prompt: Which growing threat is linked to warmer winters?
quiz.explanation: Milder winters let winter ticks survive in huge numbers on moose.

name: Common Snapping Turtle
range: Ponds, marshes and slow rivers from southern Canada east of the Rockies to the Gulf of Mexico
tagline: A dinosaur-looking survivor of the pond
lede: With a jagged shell, a long saw-toothed tail and a hooked beak, the snapping turtle looks like it walked out of the age of dinosaurs. Its lineage is ancient, and its reputation is fierce, but underwater it is a shy animal that would rather swim away.
home: Snapping turtles live in almost any fresh water with a soft bottom: ponds, marshes, lakes and slow rivers, from Nova Scotia and southern Ontario to the Gulf Coast. They spend most of their time buried in mud with just their eyes and nostrils showing.
anatomy: The common snapping turtle has a large head, a powerful hooked beak and long neck that can shoot forward surprisingly far, reaching nearly halfway back along its own shell. The top shell, or carapace, has three ridges of bumps that wear smoother with age and is often coated with algae, which helps with camouflage. The bottom shell, the plastron, is small and cross-shaped, leaving the legs free but offering little protection, which is why snappers rely on their bite. Their long tail has a row of saw-like plates along the top. Snappers have strong claws for digging and walking along the bottom; they are poor swimmers compared with many turtles and usually walk underwater instead. They have good night vision and an excellent sense of smell, and can sense vibrations through the water. Their bite is strong, but they rarely bite anything they don't intend to eat.
life: Snappers eat nearly anything: water plants, fish, frogs, insects, small birds and carrion, which makes them valuable pond cleaners. In the north they spend months beneath the ice, barely moving, and can live for decades. Females may not breed until they are 15 to 20 years old.
family: Snapping turtles mate in spring and summer, often in the water. In late May and June, females leave the water to find sunny, sandy or gravelly spots to dig nests, often road shoulders, railway beds or gardens, sometimes travelling more than a kilometre. A female digs a flask-shaped hole with her back legs and lays between about 20 and 40 round, white eggs, sometimes more, then covers them and leaves. Raccoons, skunks and foxes dig up many nests. Those that survive hatch in late summer or early autumn; in the coldest places the hatchlings may stay in the nest over winter. Nest temperature decides their sex: cooler and warmer extremes produce females, while middle temperatures produce males. The hatchlings, about the size of a coin, head straight for water. Very few survive to adulthood.
remarkable: Unlike most turtles, a snapper can't pull fully into its small shell. On land, where it can't swim away, it defends itself with a lightning-fast strike, which is where its name comes from. The temperature of the nest decides whether eggs hatch as males or females.
outlook: Snapping turtles are listed as Special Concern in Canada. Because they mature so slowly, losing even a few adults hurts a population. Many females are killed by cars while crossing roads to nest each June. Helping one across, in the direction it's heading, can save decades of life.
people: Snapping turtles have a fearsome reputation, but most people never encounter one unless they meet a female crossing a road in June. In many places, especially Ontario, people help them cross safely: lifting them carefully by the back of the shell with both hands, or nudging them along with a car mat, always in the direction they were going. Picking one up by the tail can hurt its spine. Some Indigenous creation stories describe the world being formed on the back of a great turtle, and North America is called Turtle Island by many Indigenous peoples. Snapping turtles have been hunted for food in parts of their range, and in Ontario hunting them was finally banned in 2017 because adults are so slow to replace. Turtle rescue centres now treat injured turtles and even incubate eggs from females killed on roads.
didYouKnow: Snapping turtles can't easily breathe while buried under winter ice, so they absorb some oxygen from the water through skin in their throat and rear end.

quiz.prompt: Why do snapping turtles snap on land?
choices: Their shell is too small to hide in
They can't see well in daylight
quiz.explanation: They can't retract fully into their small shell, so on land they defend themselves by striking.

quiz.prompt: What decides whether a hatchling is male or female?
choices: The time of year it hatches
quiz.explanation: Like many turtles, snappers have temperature-dependent sex determination.

quiz.prompt: What is a major threat to nesting females?
choices: Being hit by cars crossing roads
quiz.explanation: Females often cross roads in June to lay eggs, and many are killed by traffic.

name: Spring Peeper
range: Woodlands and wetlands of eastern North America, from Manitoba to the Maritimes and south to Florida
tagline: A thumbnail-sized frog that freezes solid
lede: When the first warm rain falls on melting snow, the night fills with high, bell-like 'peep! peep!' calls. That chorus, one of the first signs of spring in eastern Canada, comes from frogs small enough to sit on a coin.
home: Spring peepers live in woodlands near ponds, swamps and flooded ditches across eastern North America. They spend most of the year hidden among leaf litter and low shrubs, gathering in shallow water only for a few weeks each spring to breed.
anatomy: A spring peeper is a tiny tree frog, tan, brown or grey with a darker X-shaped mark across its back and a dark band between the eyes. Its skin can lighten or darken slightly to match its surroundings. Its fingers and toes end in round, sticky pads that let it climb grass stems and shrubs, although it spends most of its time near the ground. A male has a dark throat and a vocal sac that inflates like a balloon, almost as big as the frog itself, when it calls; the sac amplifies the sound so a single peeper can be heard far away. Like other frogs, the peeper breathes through its lungs and through its moist skin, and drinks by absorbing water through the skin of its belly. Its large eyes face forward and sideways, helping it judge distance when it leaps on insects.
life: Peepers hunt at night for small insects and spiders, climbing with sticky toe pads. Males call from the water's edge by inflating a throat sac like a bubblegum balloon. A full chorus can be heard from more than a kilometre away. Eggs hatch into tadpoles that become frogs by summer.
family: In early spring, as soon as ice melts from ponds and flooded woods, males gather and call through the night. Each 'peep' takes a lot of energy, and males may call thousands of times an evening. Females choose males, often preferring faster or louder calls. Mating happens in shallow water, where the female lays around 800 to 1,000 eggs, one at a time or in small clusters, attached to underwater plants. The eggs hatch in about a week. The tadpoles feed on algae and tiny bits of plant matter and change into tiny frogs in two to three months, leaving the water in early summer. Many breeding pools are temporary and dry up by midsummer, which keeps out fish that would eat eggs and tadpoles, but also means tadpoles race against the water drying up.
remarkable: Spring peepers survive winter by partly freezing. Ice forms in their body, their heart stops, and they stop breathing. Their liver floods their cells with glucose, which acts like antifreeze and protects them. When the thaw comes, they warm up and hop away.
outlook: Spring peepers are still common, but like many amphibians they depend on small, temporary wetlands that are easily drained or filled in. Protecting vernal pools and keeping pesticides out of wet areas helps them and many other species.
people: For many people in eastern Canada and the United States, the first peepers of the year are a beloved sign that winter is truly over, and in New England they are sometimes called 'pinkletinks'. Because they rely on small seasonal wetlands, peepers are used in volunteer frog-call surveys run in many provinces and states. Volunteers drive set routes on spring nights, stopping to listen and record which frog species are calling and how loudly, giving scientists a picture of how wetlands are faring year to year. Scientists studying how animals survive freezing have also learned a lot from frogs like peepers and wood frogs. Their natural antifreeze is of interest to medical researchers looking for better ways to preserve human organs and tissues for transplant.
didYouKnow: Its scientific name, crucifer, means 'cross-bearer', after the dark X-shaped mark on its back.

quiz.prompt: What mark does a spring peeper have on its back?
quiz.explanation: The X-shaped mark gives it the scientific name crucifer, 'cross-bearer'.

quiz.prompt: How do spring peepers survive winter?
choices: They partly freeze, protected by glucose
They live deep in warm caves
They stay active under the ice
quiz.explanation: Glucose acts like antifreeze in their cells while ice forms in their bodies.

quiz.prompt: When are peepers usually heard calling?
quiz.explanation: Their chorus is one of the first sounds of spring in eastern North America.

charities.blurb: Protects amphibian populations through education, research and habitat projects.

name: American Lobster
range: Rocky seafloor of the North Atlantic coast, from Labrador to North Carolina
tagline: An armored giant that tastes with its legs
lede: The American lobster is the heaviest crustacean on Earth. The record holder, caught off Nova Scotia, weighed more than 20 kilograms. Lobsters can live for decades, perhaps much longer, growing a little bigger every time they shed their shells.
home: American lobsters live on rocky and muddy seafloors along the Atlantic coast, from shallow coves to depths of several hundred metres. The Gulf of Maine and Canada's Maritime provinces are the heart of their range and of a huge fishery.
anatomy: An American lobster has a hard outer skeleton made of chitin and calcium, ten legs, and a long, muscular tail that ends in a fan. The first pair of legs carries the claws: a heavy, blunt crusher claw for breaking shells and a thinner cutter claw with sharp teeth for tearing. Lobsters can be right- or left-'handed', depending on which side the crusher grows. Their eyes sit on movable stalks and are good at detecting motion in dim light, though not detail. Long antennae feel their surroundings, while the short, branched antennules sample the water for scents, and tiny hairs on their walking legs and mouthparts taste food. Lobsters breathe through feathery gills tucked under the shell along their sides. Their blood is colourless or slightly blue because, like an octopus, they use copper-based hemocyanin to carry oxygen.
life: Lobsters hide in crevices by day and come out at night to eat fish, clams, crabs, sea urchins and worms. To grow, a lobster must molt: it cracks open its shell, wriggles out, and waits for a new soft shell to harden. Young lobsters molt many times a year.
family: A female lobster mates soon after she molts, while her shell is still soft. She stores sperm and later fertilises her eggs as she lays them, gluing thousands to the underside of her tail, where they are called 'berries'. A large female can carry tens of thousands of eggs. She carries and cleans them for about 9 to 11 months, fanning them with water. When they hatch, the tiny larvae float near the surface for several weeks, drifting with the currents, molting several times; most are eaten by fish. Survivors settle to the bottom, where they hide in rocky crevices. Lobsters grow slowly and may take five to eight years to reach the size allowed for harvest. Older lobsters molt less often, perhaps once every year or two, and big ones may be decades old.
remarkable: Lobsters taste with tiny hairs on their legs and smell with their short antennae. They have one big crusher claw and one slim cutter claw, and they can regrow lost limbs. Their dark blue-green shells turn red when cooked, because heat releases a red pigment called astaxanthin.
outlook: The American lobster is not endangered, and careful rules like releasing egg-bearing females have kept the fishery strong. But warming water is pushing lobsters northward, and southern New England populations have collapsed while Canadian catches rose.
people: In colonial New England and the Maritimes, lobsters were so abundant they washed up on beaches in piles and were fed to servants and prisoners and used as fertiliser. That changed in the 1800s with canning and railways, which let lobster be shipped inland, and today it is a luxury food and one of the most valuable fisheries in Canada and the United States, central to the economy and identity of many coastal towns. Fishers use rules to keep stocks healthy: minimum and maximum sizes, limited licences and seasons, and the practice of notching the tail of egg-bearing females and returning them so they can keep breeding. Scientists and fishers together track how warming water is shifting lobster populations, pushing them northward toward Atlantic Canada and away from southern New England.
didYouKnow: About one lobster in two million is born bright blue because of a genetic quirk.

quiz.prompt: Why do lobsters turn red when cooked?
choices: Heat releases a red pigment called astaxanthin
They absorb color from the water
They are red all along, hidden by mud
quiz.explanation: Astaxanthin is bound to proteins in the shell until heat frees it.

quiz.prompt: How does a lobster grow bigger?
choices: It molts, shedding its old shell
It adds new rings to its shell
It stops growing after one year
quiz.explanation: Lobsters must molt and grow a new shell each time they get larger.

quiz.prompt: How do lobsters taste their food?
choices: With tiny hairs on their legs
quiz.explanation: Sensory hairs on their legs let lobsters taste what they walk on.

name: Snow Leopard
range: High mountains of 12 countries in Central and South Asia, including the Himalayas and Altai
tagline: The ghost of the mountains
lede: Snow leopards are so well hidden and so rare that many people who live in their mountains never see one. Smoky-grey fur with dark rosettes blends perfectly into rock and snow, earning this big cat its nickname: the ghost of the mountains.
home: Snow leopards roam steep, rocky slopes usually between 3,000 and 4,500 metres, across the Himalayas, the Tibetan Plateau, the Pamirs and the Altai. A single cat may patrol a territory of hundreds of square kilometres.
anatomy: The snow leopard is a medium-sized big cat with a thick, smoky-grey to cream coat covered in dark rosettes and spots. Its fur can be up to 12 centimetres long on the belly, and its tail, almost as long as its body, is thick and furry. Its paws are large and wide, with fur on the soles that keeps them warm and spreads its weight on snow. Its forelimbs are short and powerful and its hind limbs long, giving it strength and agility for leaping across rocky slopes. The large nasal cavity warms cold air before it reaches the lungs. Its eyes are pale green or grey, unusual among big cats. Snow leopards have a partly ossified voice box that doesn't allow them to roar, so they communicate with hisses, growls, mews and a puffing sound called chuffing.
life: They hunt wild sheep and goats such as blue sheep and ibex, stalking on cliffs and pouncing from above, and also eat marmots, hares and birds. Snow leopards are solitary, keeping in touch with scent marks and scrapes. Mothers raise their cubs alone for about two years.
family: Snow leopards mate in late winter, and the female gives birth after about three months, usually to two or three cubs, in a rocky den lined with her own fur. Cubs are born blind and helpless and open their eyes after about a week. They start eating meat at around two months and leave the den with their mother at about three months. For the next year and a half, she teaches them to hunt, and the family travels together across her territory. At around 18 to 22 months, the young become independent and leave to find their own range, which can be a dangerous time as they wander into areas with livestock and people. Males take no part in raising cubs. A female may have only a few litters in her lifetime.
remarkable: Everything about the snow leopard is built for cold: thick fur, a short muzzle, small ears and huge furry paws that work like snowshoes. Its long, thick tail helps with balance on cliffs and doubles as a scarf wrapped over its face. Unlike lions and tigers, it can't roar.
outlook: There are only a few thousand snow leopards left in the wild. They are threatened by poaching, retaliation killings when they take livestock, and climate change shrinking their habitat. Programs that insure herders' livestock and involve local communities have reduced conflict.
people: Snow leopards have long been part of the cultures of Central and South Asia. In parts of the Himalayas, people see them as sacred, and Buddhist monasteries in the region help protect them. It appears on the emblems of cities such as Almaty and Bishkek, and both Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan treat it as a national symbol. Because they live in such remote mountains, they were rarely photographed until camera traps became common, and researchers now use these cameras, DNA from droppings and satellite collars to study them. Herders sometimes kill snow leopards after losing livestock. Conservation groups have reduced this by helping communities build predator-proof livestock pens, set up insurance schemes that compensate losses, and earn income from crafts and wildlife tourism, giving people a reason to keep snow leopards alive.
didYouKnow: Snow leopards can leap more than 9 metres in a single bound.

quiz.prompt: Which of these can a snow leopard NOT do?
quiz.explanation: Unlike lions, tigers and jaguars, snow leopards cannot roar.

quiz.prompt: How does a snow leopard use its long tail?
choices: For balance and as a scarf against the cold
To signal danger to other cats
quiz.explanation: The thick tail helps balance on cliffs and wraps around the face for warmth.

quiz.prompt: What are the snow leopard's main prey?
choices: Wild sheep and goats like blue sheep and ibex
quiz.explanation: Blue sheep and ibex are their most important prey.

name: Red Panda
range: Temperate mountain forests of the eastern Himalayas: Nepal, India, Bhutan, Myanmar and China
tagline: The original panda
lede: The red panda was called a 'panda' about fifty years before the giant panda was. Cat-sized, rust-red and ring-tailed, it spends most of its life in the trees of misty Himalayan forests, and it isn't a bear or a raccoon, but the last living member of its own family.
home: Red pandas live in cool, damp mountain forests with a thick understory of bamboo, usually between about 2,200 and 4,800 metres. Moss-covered trees give them places to rest, and their red and white coat blends with the red moss and white lichen.
anatomy: A red panda is about the size of a large house cat, with thick rusty-red fur on its back, black legs and belly, and a long, bushy tail ringed with red and buff stripes. Its face is white with reddish 'tear' marks running from each eye, and it has upright, white-edged ears. The dark belly and legs may help camouflage it when seen from below against the dark canopy. Its fur is dense, and even the soles of its feet are furry, protecting them from cold and wet branches. Its sharp, semi-retractable claws and flexible ankles make it a superb climber. Red pandas have strong jaws and broad molar teeth for crushing bamboo, but their digestive system is short and simple, like a carnivore's, so they extract only a small fraction of the energy in what they eat.
life: Though they belong to the order of meat-eaters, red pandas eat mostly bamboo leaves and tender shoots, plus some fruit, acorns, eggs and insects. Bamboo is hard to digest, so they save energy: sleeping a lot, slowing their metabolism in cold weather, and curling their bushy tail around them like a blanket.
family: Red pandas are solitary for most of the year and meet only to mate, in winter. After a pregnancy that can last from about three to five months, because the development of the embryo can be delayed, the female gives birth in early summer to one to four cubs, usually two, in a nest in a tree hollow or rock crevice. Before birth, she gathers leaves, moss and twigs to line it. The cubs are born with thick grey-buff fur and closed eyes, and open them at around three weeks. They stay in the nest for about three months, while the mother returns regularly to feed and clean them. They are weaned at around six to eight months and stay with her until the next breeding season, when they leave to find territories of their own.
remarkable: To grip bamboo, the red panda has a 'false thumb', an extended wrist bone that works like an extra finger. Giant pandas have one too, but the two species evolved it separately. Red pandas can also turn their ankles to climb down trees head-first.
outlook: Red pandas are endangered, with perhaps fewer than 10,000 left. Forests are being cleared for farms, roads and livestock, and red pandas are poached for fur and the pet trade. Community forest guardians in Nepal now monitor and protect their habitat.
people: The red panda was described by Western science in 1825, decades before the giant panda, and the word 'panda' probably comes from a Nepali name for it. In parts of Nepal and India, red pandas appear in local beliefs and are considered good luck. They are popular in zoos around the world, and international breeding programs keep a healthy captive population. The red panda is the state animal of Sikkim in India, and the Firefox web browser's name refers to it, since 'firefox' is one of its nicknames. In Nepal, the Red Panda Network trains local 'forest guardians', who monitor red pandas, help restore forest, and teach communities about them. Ecotourism treks to see wild red pandas give villagers income from protecting forests rather than clearing them.
didYouKnow: Red pandas mark their territory with scent glands on the soles of their feet.
