choices: It isn't closely related; it has its own family
It is a baby giant panda
It is a type of bear
It is a giant panda's cousin in the raccoon family
quiz.explanation: Red pandas are the only living members of the family Ailuridae.

quiz.prompt: What helps a red panda grip bamboo?
choices: An extended wrist bone, a 'false thumb'
Hooked claws on its back feet
quiz.explanation: A wrist bone that acts like a thumb lets it hold bamboo stems.

quiz.prompt: What makes up most of a red panda's diet?
quiz.explanation: Bamboo leaves and shoots make up the vast majority of what it eats.

charities.name: Red Panda Network
charities.blurb: Trains local 'forest guardians' and restores red panda habitat in Nepal.

name: Sunda Pangolin
range: Forests and plantations of Southeast Asia, from Myanmar and Vietnam to Borneo, Sumatra and Java
tagline: A walking pinecone with a sticky tongue
lede: Pangolins are the only mammals covered in scales. When threatened, a Sunda pangolin rolls into a tight, armored ball that even a tiger struggles to open. Sadly, that defense is no protection against people, and pangolins are among the most trafficked wild mammals in the world.
home: Sunda pangolins live in tropical forests across Southeast Asia, and also in gardens and plantations. They are nocturnal, spending the day curled up in burrows or tree hollows, and are excellent climbers that use their tails to grip branches.
anatomy: The Sunda pangolin is covered from head to tail in overlapping brownish scales, except for its face, belly and inner legs, which are covered in skin and sparse hair. The scales are made of keratin and grow throughout its life, worn down as it digs and climbs. It has a small, cone-shaped head, tiny eyes and poor eyesight, but an excellent sense of smell for finding ant and termite nests. Its front feet have long, curved claws for ripping into nests, so it walks on its knuckles or on its hind legs to protect them. Its long, sticky tongue starts deep in its chest and is coated with thick saliva. Without teeth, it relies on a muscular stomach with tough spines and swallowed stones to grind its food. Its prehensile tail can grip branches, helping it climb trees with ease.
life: Pangolins eat ants and termites, tearing open nests with strong front claws. They have no teeth. Instead they catch insects with a sticky tongue that can be longer than their head and body, anchored deep in the chest. They swallow small stones that help grind food in the stomach.
family: Sunda pangolins live alone and meet only to mate. After a pregnancy of around six months, the female usually gives birth to a single baby, sometimes two, often in a burrow or tree hollow. The newborn's scales are soft at first and harden within a couple of days. For the first weeks, the baby stays in the den while the mother forages. Later it rides on her back or tail as she travels and climbs, gripping tightly. If danger threatens, the mother curls into a ball around her young one, sheltering it inside her armour. The young pangolin learns to find food by following its mother and is weaned at about three or four months, staying with her until it is ready to live on its own. Pangolins breed slowly, so populations recover poorly from hunting.
remarkable: A pangolin's scales are made of keratin, the same material as your fingernails, and they overlap like roof tiles. Mothers carry their single baby on their tail, and the baby clings on and can be wrapped up safely when the mother rolls into a ball.
outlook: The Sunda pangolin is critically endangered. Hundreds of thousands of pangolins have been taken from the wild for their meat and for scales used in traditional medicine, even though their scales have no proven medical value. All international trade in pangolins is banned.
people: Pangolins have been eaten as bushmeat and used in traditional medicine across Asia for a very long time, with their scales wrongly believed to cure ailments from poor circulation to skin disease. In recent decades, demand has turned this into a vast illegal trade, with tonnes of scales seized at ports, and the Sunda pangolin is now critically endangered. Since 2017, all eight pangolin species have been listed on Appendix I of CITES, which bans international commercial trade, and China removed pangolin scales from its official list of traditional medicines in 2020. Rescue centres in Vietnam, Indonesia and Malaysia care for pangolins confiscated from traffickers, and some are released back into protected forests. World Pangolin Day, held each February, raises awareness of these little-known animals.
didYouKnow: The word 'pangolin' comes from the Malay word penggulung, meaning 'roller'.

quiz.prompt: What are pangolin scales made of?
quiz.explanation: Pangolin scales are keratin, the same protein in human nails and hair.

quiz.prompt: How does a pangolin defend itself?
choices: It rolls into a tight, scaly ball
quiz.explanation: Rolled up, its overlapping scales protect its soft belly.

quiz.prompt: Why are pangolins so heavily trafficked?
choices: For their meat and scales used in traditional medicine
quiz.explanation: Illegal demand for meat and scales has driven pangolins toward extinction.

charities.name: Save Pangolins
charities.blurb: Funds pangolin research, rescue and anti-trafficking work across Asia and Africa.

name: African Bush Elephant
range: Savannas, grasslands and woodlands across sub-Saharan Africa
tagline: The largest animal that walks the Earth
lede: No land animal alive is bigger than the African bush elephant. A big bull can weigh as much as a city bus. Yet elephants are also among the most social and emotional animals on Earth, living in close families led by wise old females.
home: Bush elephants live across much of sub-Saharan Africa, from open savanna to woodland and even desert edges in Namibia and Mali. They travel long distances between water and food, and their old migration paths connect many national parks.
life: Elephants eat grasses, leaves, bark, roots and fruit, up to around 150 kilograms a day, and spend most of their waking hours feeding. Herds are led by a matriarch, usually the oldest female, whose memory of water holes can mean survival in a drought. Males leave as teenagers.
remarkable: An elephant's trunk has tens of thousands of muscles and can lift a log or pick up a single peanut. Elephants talk in deep rumbles, many too low for us to hear, that travel kilometres through the air and ground. Their huge ears flap to release heat.
outlook: African bush elephants are endangered. Poaching for ivory killed hundreds of thousands in recent decades, and growing farms and towns squeeze their habitat and cause conflict with people. Where protection is strong, like in parts of Kenya and Botswana, numbers have recovered.
didYouKnow: Research suggests elephants use distinct calls for individual family members, much like names.

quiz.prompt: Who usually leads an elephant herd?
quiz.explanation: A matriarch leads her family using decades of experience.

quiz.prompt: What is one purpose of an elephant's huge ears?
quiz.explanation: Flapping their ears helps elephants cool down in the African heat.

quiz.prompt: How do elephants communicate over long distances?
choices: Deep, low rumbles that travel kilometres
Flashing their tusks in the sun
quiz.explanation: Elephant rumbles, many below human hearing, carry far through air and ground.

charities.name: Save the Elephants
charities.blurb: Researches elephant behavior and works to end the ivory trade in Kenya and beyond.

name: Cheetah
range: Grasslands and savannas of eastern and southern Africa, plus a tiny population in Iran
tagline: Built for a few seconds of pure speed
lede: The cheetah is the fastest land animal on Earth, reaching about 100 km/h in a few seconds. Everything about it, from its slim body to its oversized heart and lungs, is designed for one explosive sprint.
home: Cheetahs need wide open country where they can see prey and chase it: grasslands, savannas and dry woodlands. Most live outside protected areas, on farmland in places like Namibia and Botswana, which makes good relations with farmers essential.
life: Cheetahs hunt in daylight, often in the morning and late afternoon, to avoid lions and hyenas that hunt at night. They stalk gazelles and impala, sprint, trip the prey with a paw, then must rest. Bigger predators often steal their kills, so they eat quickly.
remarkable: A cheetah's flexible spine works like a spring, and its claws only partly retract, gripping the ground like running spikes. Its long tail acts as a rudder in sharp turns. The black 'tear lines' under its eyes may cut glare from the sun. Cheetahs can't roar, but they purr and chirp like birds.
outlook: Fewer than about 7,000 adult cheetahs remain, mostly in southern and eastern Africa; the Asiatic cheetah in Iran is down to a handful. Habitat loss, conflict with livestock farmers and illegal trade in cubs as pets are the main threats. Livestock guard dogs have reduced conflict in Namibia.
didYouKnow: A cheetah can go from standing still to about 95 km/h in only three seconds.

quiz.prompt: What may the black 'tear lines' on a cheetah's face do?
quiz.explanation: The dark lines likely cut sun glare, helping cheetahs focus on prey in daylight.

quiz.prompt: Why do cheetahs' claws only partly retract?
choices: They grip the ground like running spikes
They are too big to retract
quiz.explanation: Semi-retractable claws give extra traction during high-speed chases.

quiz.prompt: Which sound can a cheetah NOT make?
quiz.explanation: Cheetahs purr, chirp and hiss, but cannot roar.

charities.name: Cheetah Conservation Fund
charities.blurb: Works with farmers in Namibia, including breeding livestock guard dogs, to protect wild cheetahs.

name: Okapi
range: Dense rainforest of the northeastern Democratic Republic of the Congo
tagline: The forest giraffe with zebra legs
lede: With striped legs like a zebra, a velvety chocolate coat and a face like a giraffe, the okapi looks assembled from spare parts. It was so secretive that Western scientists only described it in 1901, and it's still rarely seen in the wild.
home: Okapis live only in the dense rainforests of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, especially the Ituri Forest. The striped legs break up their outline in the dappled light of the forest floor, making them nearly invisible.
life: Okapis are solitary browsers that eat leaves, buds, fruit and fungi, and they visit clay and charcoal from lightning-struck trees for minerals. They follow regular paths through the forest. A mother hides her calf in a nest of leaves for weeks, and the calf barely makes a sound.
remarkable: The okapi's closest living relative is the giraffe. Like a giraffe, it has a long, dark, flexible tongue, long enough to clean its own eyelids and ears. Okapis communicate with very low sounds that predators like leopards may not be able to hear.
outlook: Okapis are endangered. Logging, mining and armed conflict in eastern Congo destroy their forest and make protection dangerous. Rangers at the Okapi Wildlife Reserve protect them at great personal risk, and the okapi is a national symbol of the DRC.
didYouKnow: Okapi stripes are thought to help calves follow their mothers through the dark forest.

quiz.prompt: What is the okapi's closest living relative?
quiz.explanation: Despite the zebra stripes, okapis belong to the giraffe family.

quiz.prompt: Where do wild okapis live?
choices: Rainforests of the Democratic Republic of the Congo
quiz.explanation: Okapis are found only in the rainforests of the DRC.

quiz.prompt: What can an okapi do with its long tongue?
choices: Clean its own ears and eyelids
quiz.explanation: Its long, flexible tongue can reach its eyes and ears.

charities.name: Okapi Conservation Project
charities.blurb: Supports rangers and communities protecting the Okapi Wildlife Reserve.

name: Bornean Orangutan
range: Lowland rainforests and peat swamps of Borneo, in Indonesia and Malaysia
tagline: The thoughtful person of the forest
lede: 'Orangutan' comes from Malay words meaning 'person of the forest'. It's a fitting name. These great apes share about 97 percent of our DNA, use tools, and learn skills from their mothers over years of patient childhood.
home: Bornean orangutans live in rainforests and peat swamp forests on the island of Borneo. They are the largest tree-dwelling animals on Earth, moving slowly and carefully through the canopy and rarely coming down to the ground.
life: Orangutans eat mostly fruit, especially figs and durian, along with leaves, bark, flowers and insects. Every evening, each orangutan bends and weaves branches into a fresh nest to sleep in. Young orangutans stay with their mothers for about seven or eight years, the longest childhood of any animal except humans.
remarkable: Orangutans use sticks to pull seeds from spiky fruit and leaves as umbrellas, and they learn these tricks by watching. Adult males may grow large cheek pads called flanges and a throat sac that amplifies their 'long call', which can be heard a kilometre away.
outlook: Bornean orangutans are critically endangered. More than half of the population was lost between 1999 and 2015, as forests were cleared for oil palm and paper plantations, burned in fires and logged. Protected forests and rescue centres are helping, and choosing products with deforestation-free palm oil makes a difference.
didYouKnow: Because mothers have a baby only every six to eight years, orangutans are among the slowest-breeding mammals on Earth.

quiz.prompt: What does 'orangutan' mean?
quiz.explanation: It comes from Malay words meaning 'person of the forest'.

quiz.prompt: How often do orangutans build a sleeping nest?
choices: Never; they sleep on the ground
quiz.explanation: Each evening they weave a new nest of branches high in the trees.

quiz.prompt: How long do young orangutans stay with their mothers?
quiz.explanation: Orangutans have one of the longest childhoods of any animal.

charities.name: Orangutan Foundation International
charities.blurb: Runs orangutan rescue, rehabilitation and forest protection in Borneo.

name: Platypus
range: Rivers and streams of eastern Australia and Tasmania
tagline: A mammal that lays eggs and hunts by electricity
lede: When the first platypus specimen reached Britain in 1799, some scientists thought it was a hoax: a duck's bill sewn onto a mammal. It's real, and the truth is stranger than the hoax. The platypus lays eggs, hunts with an electric sense, and the males are venomous.
home: Platypuses live in freshwater rivers, creeks and lakes in eastern Australia and Tasmania, from tropical Queensland to icy alpine streams. They dig burrows in the riverbanks with entrances just above the water line.
life: Platypuses hunt at night for insect larvae, freshwater shrimp, worms and yabbies, eating around a fifth of their body weight a day. They store food in cheek pouches and grind it with rough pads, since adults have no teeth. Females lay one to three eggs and nurse the babies with milk that seeps from their skin.
remarkable: When a platypus dives, it closes its eyes, ears and nostrils. It finds prey using its soft bill, which is packed with sensors that detect the tiny electric fields made by muscles of moving animals. Males have a venomous spur on each hind ankle, painful enough to disable a dog.
outlook: The platypus is listed as near threatened. Dams, drought, land clearing and pollution damage its rivers, and many drown in illegal 'opera house' yabby traps. Healthy, flowing streams with vegetated banks are what they need most.
didYouKnow: Under ultraviolet light, platypus fur glows a blue-green color.

quiz.prompt: How does a platypus find prey with its eyes closed?
choices: It senses electric fields with its bill
quiz.explanation: Electroreceptors in its bill detect the electric signals of moving prey.

quiz.prompt: How do platypuses have babies?
choices: Babies grow in a pouch from birth
They hatch from eggs laid by the father
quiz.explanation: The platypus is a monotreme, one of the few mammals that lay eggs.

quiz.prompt: What do male platypuses have?
choices: Venomous spurs on their hind ankles
quiz.explanation: Males carry a venomous spur on each hind leg.

charities.name: WWF-Australia
charities.blurb: Works to protect Australian rivers, forests and the wildlife that depends on them.

name: Kākāpō
range: A few predator-free islands off New Zealand, such as Whenua Hou
tagline: A flightless parrot where every bird has a name
lede: The kākāpō is a moss-green parrot that can't fly, comes out at night, smells faintly of honey, and may live for decades. It is the heaviest parrot in the world, and one of the rarest birds on Earth. There are so few that every single one has a name.
home: Kākāpō once lived across New Zealand. Today they survive only on a few small islands cleared of rats, stoats and cats, such as Whenua Hou (Codfish Island) and Anchor Island, where rangers track every bird by radio.
life: Kākāpō eat leaves, seeds, roots and fruit, and they only breed in years when trees like the rimu produce a huge crop of fruit, which may happen only every two to four years. Instead of flying, they climb trees and use their wings like parachutes to glide down.
remarkable: To attract females, males dig bowl-shaped hollows on hilltops and inflate air sacs in their chests to make deep 'booming' calls that carry for kilometres, night after night. As a defense, kākāpō freeze when threatened, which worked against birds of prey but not against introduced mammals.
outlook: By 1995 only about 50 kākāpō were left. An intense recovery program, with island sanctuaries, supplementary feeding and veterinary care, has slowly lifted numbers to a couple of hundred. Each breeding season is followed closely across New Zealand.
didYouKnow: Kākāpō are thought to live for 60 years or more, one of the longest lifespans of any bird.

quiz.prompt: What makes the kākāpō unusual among parrots?
choices: It can't fly and is the heaviest parrot
quiz.explanation: It is the world's only flightless parrot and the heaviest.

quiz.prompt: How do male kākāpō attract mates?
choices: Deep booming calls from hollows they dig
quiz.explanation: Males boom from bowl-shaped hollows night after night.

quiz.prompt: What triggers a kākāpō breeding season?
choices: Years when rimu trees produce lots of fruit
quiz.explanation: They only breed in mast years when trees like rimu fruit heavily.

charities.name: Kākāpō Recovery
charities.blurb: New Zealand's Department of Conservation program that cares for every kākāpō.

name: Emperor Penguin
range: Sea ice around the coast of Antarctica
tagline: Raising chicks in the coldest place on Earth
lede: Emperor penguins do something no other animal attempts. They breed in the middle of the Antarctic winter, on sea ice, in temperatures that can fall below minus 40 degrees and winds of 150 km/h, in total darkness.
home: Emperors live around Antarctica, nesting in colonies on sea ice attached to the coast, sometimes far from open water. When they're not breeding, they hunt in the icy Southern Ocean, resting on floating ice between trips.
life: Females lay a single egg and pass it to their mate, then walk back to the sea to feed. For about two months, the male balances the egg on his feet under a warm flap of skin, eating nothing. Thousands of males huddle together, shuffling so each takes a turn in the warm middle.
remarkable: Emperors are the tallest and heaviest penguins and the deepest-diving birds: they can reach more than 500 metres and stay down for over 20 minutes. They survive the cold with dense feathers, thick fat, and a heat-exchange system in their legs and nose.
outlook: Emperor penguins depend on stable sea ice to raise their chicks. In recent years, early ice break-up has caused whole colonies to fail, and scientists project steep declines this century as Antarctica warms. Reducing greenhouse gases is the only real long-term protection.
didYouKnow: A male emperor can lose almost half his body weight while incubating the egg through winter.

quiz.prompt: Who keeps the emperor penguin egg warm?
choices: The father, balancing it on his feet
The mother, in a nest of stones
quiz.explanation: Males incubate the egg on their feet for about two months.

quiz.prompt: When do emperor penguins breed?
quiz.explanation: Emperors are the only penguins that breed through the Antarctic winter.

quiz.prompt: How do huddling males share warmth fairly?
choices: They shuffle so each takes a turn in the middle
The biggest stay in the middle
They take turns diving into the sea
quiz.explanation: The huddle slowly rotates so every penguin gets time in the warm centre.

charities.name: Antarctic and Southern Ocean Coalition
charities.blurb: Campaigns for marine protected areas and strong protection of Antarctica.

name: Polar Bear
range: Arctic sea ice and coasts of Canada, Alaska, Greenland, Norway and Russia
tagline: A bear that lives on the frozen sea
lede: The polar bear is the largest land carnivore on Earth, but it's really a creature of the sea ice. It is classified as a marine mammal, spends most of its life on frozen ocean, and can swim for days. About two-thirds of the world's polar bears live in Canada.
home: Polar bears roam the sea ice of the Arctic Ocean and surrounding seas. In places like Hudson Bay, the ice melts every summer, forcing bears ashore to wait for freeze-up. The town of Churchill, Manitoba, sees so many that it's called the polar bear capital of the world.
life: Polar bears hunt seals, especially ringed and bearded seals, waiting patiently beside breathing holes in the ice or stalking seals resting on the surface. A bear can smell a seal from more than a kilometre away. Pregnant females dig snow dens where tiny cubs are born in winter.
remarkable: Polar bears aren't really white. Their skin is black to soak up heat, and their fur is made of transparent, hollow-cored hairs that scatter light and look white. A thick layer of fat keeps them warm even while swimming in icy water.
outlook: Polar bears need sea ice to hunt, and Arctic sea ice is shrinking as the climate warms. Longer ice-free seasons mean longer fasts and thinner bears, and some populations have already declined. Their future depends on how fast global emissions fall.
didYouKnow: Polar bears have small bumps called papillae on their paw pads that grip the ice like non-slip soles.

quiz.prompt: What color is a polar bear's skin?
quiz.explanation: Black skin absorbs heat; the transparent fur only looks white.

quiz.prompt: What is the polar bear's main prey?
quiz.explanation: Ringed and bearded seals make up most of a polar bear's diet.

quiz.prompt: Why is sea ice so important to polar bears?
choices: It's their platform for hunting seals
They drink it as fresh water
It keeps them hidden from orcas
They sleep inside it all summer
quiz.explanation: Without sea ice, polar bears can't reach the seals they depend on.

charities.name: Polar Bears International
charities.blurb: Researches polar bears and the sea ice they need, based partly in Churchill, Manitoba.

name: Narwhal
range: Arctic waters of Canada, Greenland, Norway and Russia
tagline: The unicorn of the sea
lede: For centuries, Europeans sold narwhal tusks as unicorn horns, worth more than their weight in gold. The truth is just as magical: a whale with a single spiralling tooth up to 3 metres long, living among the ice floes of the high Arctic.
home: Narwhals live year-round in Arctic waters, mostly in the Canadian Arctic and around Greenland. In summer they gather in ice-free bays and fjords; in winter they move offshore under thick pack ice, surfacing through cracks to breathe.
life: Narwhals travel in groups and eat Greenland halibut, Arctic cod, squid and shrimp, often swallowing prey whole by suction. They are some of the deepest-diving mammals, reaching more than 1,500 metres in winter to hunt in total darkness.
remarkable: The tusk is actually a tooth, usually the left canine, that grows straight out through the upper lip in a left-handed spiral. Most males have one; a few females do, and rarely a narwhal grows two. The tusk may be used to show off to rivals and to sense the water around it.
outlook: Narwhals are currently listed as least concern, but they are very sensitive to change. Melting sea ice opens the Arctic to shipping, noise and new predators like orcas, and their specialised diet makes it hard to adapt. Inuit communities hunt narwhal sustainably and help monitor them.
didYouKnow: Narwhals have no dorsal fin, which may help them swim under ice without scraping.

quiz.prompt: What is a narwhal's tusk?
quiz.explanation: The tusk is a tooth, usually the left canine, that grows through the lip.

quiz.prompt: Which narwhals usually have a tusk?
quiz.explanation: Most males grow a tusk; only a few females do.

quiz.prompt: How deep can narwhals dive?
quiz.explanation: Narwhals are among the deepest-diving mammals in the ocean.

charities.name: WWF
charities.blurb: Works with Arctic communities to protect narwhals, sea ice habitat and marine life.

name: Blue Whale
range: All the world's oceans, from the Antarctic to the North Atlantic and Pacific
tagline: The largest animal that has ever lived
lede: Bigger than any dinosaur, the blue whale is the largest animal known to have ever existed. It can grow to around 30 metres long and weigh as much as 30 elephants. Its heart alone weighs around 180 kilograms.
home: Blue whales live in every ocean. Many travel between cold, food-rich feeding grounds near the poles and warmer waters where they give birth. Some populations, like one in the northern Indian Ocean, may stay in one region year-round.
life: Incredibly, the biggest animal on Earth eats one of the smallest: krill, tiny shrimp-like animals. A blue whale lunges into a swarm with its mouth open, gulping a volume of water larger than its own body, then pushes it out through baleen plates that trap the krill. It can eat several tonnes a day.
remarkable: Blue whale calls are among the loudest sounds made by any animal, deep enough that much of it is below human hearing, and can travel hundreds of kilometres underwater. A newborn calf is about 7 metres long and gains around 90 kilograms a day on its mother's rich milk.
outlook: Whaling killed hundreds of thousands of blue whales in the 20th century, leaving some populations at a few percent of their original size. They have been protected since 1966 and are slowly recovering, but ship strikes, entanglement in fishing gear and ocean noise remain threats.
didYouKnow: Blue whales can live 80 to 90 years, which scientists estimate by counting layers in their earwax plugs, a bit like tree rings.

quiz.prompt: What does the blue whale mainly eat?
quiz.explanation: The largest animal on Earth survives on tiny shrimp-like krill.

quiz.prompt: How does a blue whale filter its food from the water?
choices: Through baleen plates in its mouth
quiz.explanation: Baleen plates trap krill while water is pushed out.

quiz.prompt: Since when have blue whales been protected from hunting?
quiz.explanation: Blue whales were protected internationally in 1966 after heavy whaling.

charities.name: Whale and Dolphin Conservation
charities.blurb: Fights threats to whales and dolphins, from whaling to ship strikes and entanglement.

name: Common Octopus
range: Coastal waters of the Mediterranean and eastern Atlantic
tagline: Three hearts, blue blood and a brain in every arm
lede: The common octopus is about as alien as life on Earth gets: three hearts, blue blood, no bones, and skin that can change color in a fraction of a second. It's also remarkably clever, able to solve puzzles, open jars and escape from aquarium tanks.
home: Common octopuses live along rocky coasts, reefs and seagrass beds of the Mediterranean and the eastern Atlantic, usually in fairly shallow water. Each one makes a den in a crevice or shell pile, often decorated with the empty shells of its meals.
life: Octopuses hunt mostly at dusk and night, catching crabs, clams and snails. They pry open shells or drill a hole and inject venom that softens the prey. They live fast: most survive just one to two years. A female guards her eggs for weeks without eating, and dies soon after they hatch.
remarkable: About two-thirds of an octopus's neurons are in its arms, so each arm can taste, touch and react partly on its own. Special skin cells change color and texture to match rock or seaweed instantly. When escape fails, it squirts a cloud of ink and jets away.
outlook: The common octopus is not considered threatened, but it is heavily fished, and scientists worry about plans to farm octopuses, given their intelligence and solitary nature. Several countries now recognise octopuses as sentient in animal-welfare law.
didYouKnow: An octopus's blood is blue because it uses copper-based hemocyanin to carry oxygen, instead of iron-based hemoglobin.

quiz.prompt: How many hearts does an octopus have?
quiz.explanation: Two hearts pump blood through the gills and one through the body.

quiz.prompt: Where are most of an octopus's neurons?
quiz.explanation: About two-thirds of its neurons are in its arms.

quiz.prompt: What happens to a mother octopus after her eggs hatch?
choices: She raises the young for a year
She lays another batch right away
She leaves to find a new den
quiz.explanation: Females guard their eggs without eating and die soon after they hatch.

charities.name: Oceana
charities.blurb: Campaigns to protect ocean habitats and end overfishing.

name: Leatherback Sea Turtle
range: Oceans worldwide, from tropical nesting beaches to the cold waters off Nova Scotia
tagline: The jellyfish hunter that crosses oceans
lede: The leatherback is the largest turtle on Earth and one of the great ocean wanderers. Instead of a hard shell, it wears a flexible, leathery carapace, and it travels thousands of kilometres from tropical beaches to cold northern seas, following the jellyfish it eats.
home: Leatherbacks have the widest range of any reptile. They nest on tropical beaches in places like Trinidad, Costa Rica and Gabon, then swim into cold waters, including off Nova Scotia and Newfoundland each summer, where jellyfish are plentiful.
life: Leatherbacks eat almost nothing but jellyfish, which are mostly water, so they must eat huge amounts. Their mouths and throats are lined with backward-pointing spines that keep slippery jellyfish from escaping. Females come ashore at night to dig nests and lay dozens of eggs.
remarkable: Unlike most reptiles, leatherbacks can keep their bodies warmer than the water around them, thanks to their large size, a thick layer of fat and clever blood vessels in their flippers. They can dive deeper than 1,000 metres, deeper than many whales.
outlook: Leatherbacks are vulnerable worldwide, and Pacific populations have crashed. They are often caught by accident in fishing gear, their eggs are taken, and they mistake floating plastic bags for jellyfish. Beach protection and turtle-safe fishing gear are helping some Atlantic populations.
didYouKnow: Leatherback turtles have been around in some form for over 100 million years, since the age of dinosaurs.

quiz.prompt: What do leatherbacks mainly eat?
quiz.explanation: Leatherbacks live almost entirely on jellyfish.

quiz.prompt: How is a leatherback's shell different from other turtles'?
choices: It's flexible and leathery, not hard
It has no shell at all
quiz.explanation: Its carapace is leathery skin over small bones, not hard plates.

quiz.prompt: Why are plastic bags dangerous to leatherbacks?
choices: They look like jellyfish and get eaten
quiz.explanation: Floating plastic bags are easily mistaken for jellyfish.

charities.name: Sea Turtle Conservancy
charities.blurb: Protects nesting beaches and tracks sea turtles across the Atlantic and Caribbean.

name: Whale Shark
range: Warm tropical oceans worldwide, gathering at places like Ningaloo Reef and the Yucatán
tagline: The gentle giant with a starry back
lede: The whale shark is the biggest fish in the sea, as long as a bus, yet it's harmless to people. Swimmers who meet one see a vast, spotted body gliding slowly past, its wide mouth open, sieving the water for food far too small to see.
home: Whale sharks roam warm tropical oceans around the world, often far out at sea and deep underwater. At certain times of year they gather where food is plentiful: Ningaloo Reef in Western Australia, the Yucatán coast of Mexico, the Maldives and the Philippines.
life: Whale sharks are filter feeders. They eat plankton, krill, fish eggs and small fish, either swimming slowly with their mouth open or sucking in water while hanging upright. Their gills have spongy filter pads that sieve out food. Much of their life, including where they give birth, is still a mystery.
remarkable: Each whale shark's pattern of pale spots and stripes is unique, like a fingerprint. Researchers and divers photograph the spots behind the gills, and computer software originally designed to map stars matches them to identify individuals across years and oceans.
outlook: Whale sharks are endangered. They grow and breed slowly, and numbers have fallen because of fishing, accidental catch in nets, and collisions with ships. Well-managed tourism, like at Ningaloo, now makes a living whale shark far more valuable than a dead one.
didYouKnow: A whale shark's mouth can be more than a metre wide and contains thousands of tiny teeth that it doesn't use for eating.

quiz.prompt: What kind of animal is a whale shark?
choices: A fish, the largest in the sea
quiz.explanation: Despite the name, it's a shark, and the world's biggest fish.

quiz.prompt: What does a whale shark eat?
choices: Plankton and tiny animals it filters from the water
quiz.explanation: It's a gentle filter feeder that sieves plankton and small prey.

quiz.prompt: How do researchers tell individual whale sharks apart?
choices: By their unique pattern of spots
By the shape of their teeth
By the color of their eyes
quiz.explanation: Each spot pattern is unique, like a fingerprint.

charities.name: Marine Megafauna Foundation
charities.blurb: Researches and protects whale sharks, manta rays and other ocean giants.

name: Strawberry Poison Frog
range: Lowland rainforests of Nicaragua, Costa Rica and Panama
tagline: A tiny jewel that's a devoted parent
lede: Barely 2 centimetres long and bright as a candy, the strawberry poison frog is impossible to miss on the rainforest floor. That's exactly the point. Its color warns every predator: I'm toxic. Don't even try.
home: Strawberry poison frogs live in humid lowland rainforests from Nicaragua to Panama, hopping through leaf litter by day. In Panama's Bocas del Toro islands, isolated populations evolved into more than a dozen color forms, from red with blue legs to green, orange and yellow.
life: These frogs eat ants and mites. The poison on their skin, called alkaloids, comes from these prey, so frogs raised in captivity on other insects aren't toxic. Males call from perches to defend territories, and parents share the work of raising their young.
remarkable: After the eggs hatch, the mother carries each tadpole on her back up into the trees, placing it in its own tiny pool of water cupped in a bromeliad leaf. Then she returns every few days to lay unfertilised eggs for it to eat. Few frogs work so hard for their young.
outlook: The species is still common, but its forests are being cleared for farming and development, and some island color forms have tiny ranges. Collecting for the pet trade is another pressure. Like all amphibians, it's also threatened by the deadly chytrid fungus.
didYouKnow: The red-and-blue form is nicknamed the 'blue jeans' frog because its legs look like it's wearing denim.

quiz.prompt: Where does the frog's poison come from?
choices: The ants and mites it eats
It's born with it, whatever it eats
quiz.explanation: Toxins come from its diet; captive frogs fed other insects are harmless.

quiz.prompt: What does the mother feed her tadpoles?
choices: Nothing; they find their own food
quiz.explanation: She returns to each tadpole to lay unfertilised eggs as food.

quiz.prompt: Where are the tadpoles raised?
choices: In tiny pools held by bromeliad leaves
quiz.explanation: The mother carries each tadpole up to its own little bromeliad pool.

charities.name: Amphibian Ark
charities.blurb: Coordinates rescue and conservation breeding for amphibians facing extinction.

name: Brown-throated Sloth
range: Rainforests from Honduras to Bolivia and northern Argentina
tagline: A slow life, perfectly lived
lede: The brown-throated sloth moves so slowly that algae grows in its fur. It's not lazy; it's efficient. Living on a diet of leaves that provides very little energy, the sloth has turned slowness into a survival strategy that has worked for millions of years.
home: These three-toed sloths live in the rainforests of Central and South America, from Honduras to Bolivia. They spend almost their whole lives hanging upside-down in the canopy, gripping branches with long, curved claws.
life: Sloths eat leaves, especially from cecropia trees. Their large, multi-chambered stomach can take weeks to digest a meal. To save energy they move slowly, sleep a lot and let their body temperature drop at night. About once a week, they climb all the way down to the ground to poop.
remarkable: Green algae grow in grooves in sloth hair, helping them blend into the treetops, and moths live in their fur too. Three-toed sloths have extra neck bones, letting them turn their heads about 270 degrees. Surprisingly, they are good swimmers.
outlook: The brown-throated sloth is still widespread, but deforestation breaks up its forest, forcing sloths onto the ground, roads and power lines where they're in danger. Wildlife bridges and power-line insulation in Costa Rica are helping them get around safely.
didYouKnow: A sloth's slow movements make it hard for eagles and jaguars, which hunt by spotting motion, to notice them.

quiz.prompt: Why does a sloth's fur often look green?
choices: It's dyed by the fruit it eats
quiz.explanation: Algae grows in grooves in the hair and helps with camouflage.

quiz.prompt: How often do sloths climb down to the ground?
choices: About once a week, to poop
quiz.explanation: They descend roughly once a week to relieve themselves.

quiz.prompt: Why do sloths move so slowly?
choices: Their leafy diet gives them very little energy
quiz.explanation: Slow movement saves energy on a low-calorie diet of leaves.

charities.name: The Sloth Conservation Foundation
charities.blurb: Builds wildlife bridges and researches sloths in Costa Rica.

name: Jaguar
range: From northern Mexico through the Amazon to northern Argentina
tagline: The water-loving king of the Americas
lede: The jaguar is the largest cat in the Americas and the third largest in the world. Unlike most cats, it loves water. In Brazil's Pantanal wetlands, jaguars swim rivers, hunt caimans and fish, and doze on sandbanks in the afternoon heat.
home: Jaguars live in rainforests, swamps, grasslands and dry forests from Mexico to Argentina, with strongholds in the Amazon and the Pantanal. They prefer to stay close to rivers and lakes, and they need large connected areas of wild land.
life: Jaguars eat almost anything they can catch: capybaras, deer, peccaries, caimans, turtles, fish and even anacondas. They usually hunt alone at dawn and dusk, stalking quietly and ambushing prey. Females raise their cubs for about two years.
remarkable: For its size, the jaguar has one of the most powerful bites of any big cat. Instead of going for the throat, it often kills with a single bite through the skull, and can crack a turtle's shell. Its rosettes have dots inside them, which leopards' rosettes lack.
outlook: Jaguars are near threatened and have already vanished from about half of their original range. Forest clearing for ranching and farming, fires, and conflict with cattle ranchers are the biggest threats. Wildlife corridors connecting protected areas are key to their future.
didYouKnow: The name 'jaguar' is often traced to the Tupi-Guarani word yaguara, said to mean something like 'one who kills with a single leap'.

quiz.prompt: How can you tell a jaguar from a leopard?
choices: Jaguar rosettes have spots inside them
quiz.explanation: Jaguar rosettes usually contain small dots; leopard rosettes don't.

quiz.prompt: How do jaguars often kill their prey?
choices: With a bite through the skull
By chasing it until it's exhausted
quiz.explanation: Their powerful bite can pierce skulls and turtle shells.

quiz.prompt: What do jaguars think of water?
choices: They love it and are strong swimmers
quiz.explanation: Jaguars swim well and hunt caimans and fish in rivers.

charities.name: Panthera
charities.blurb: Global wild cat conservation, including the Jaguar Corridor Initiative.

name: Andean Condor
range: The Andes mountains and Pacific coast of South America, from Venezuela to Tierra del Fuego
tagline: The bird that barely needs to flap
lede: With wings stretching more than 3 metres, the Andean condor is one of the largest flying birds in the world. It's also one of the most efficient. One tracked condor flew more than 170 kilometres over five hours without flapping its wings once.
home: Andean condors live along the Andes mountains, from Venezuela to the southern tip of South America, and along nearby Pacific coasts. They nest on high cliff ledges and soar over open grasslands and mountains in search of food.
life: Condors are scavengers. They eat carrion, mostly large dead animals like guanacos, cattle, and on the coast, dead sea lions and whales. They help keep ecosystems clean. Pairs mate for life and raise just one chick every two years, caring for it for over a year.
remarkable: Condors ride rising currents of warm air and wind deflected off mountains, flapping during only about one percent of their flight time, mostly during take-off. They can soar to over 5,000 metres. Males have a fleshy comb on their heads and a ruff of white feathers around their necks.
outlook: Condors are vulnerable because they breed so slowly. Many are poisoned by bait set out for predators or by lead from bullets in carcasses, and some are shot. Captive breeding and release programs have returned condors to areas where they had vanished.
didYouKnow: The Andean condor is a national symbol of Bolivia, Chile, Colombia, Ecuador and Peru.

quiz.prompt: What do Andean condors eat?
quiz.explanation: Condors are scavengers that feed on carcasses.

quiz.prompt: How do condors fly so efficiently?
choices: They soar on rising air and rarely flap
quiz.explanation: Condors flap only about one percent of the time, riding air currents.

quiz.prompt: How often do condors raise a chick?
choices: About one chick every two years
quiz.explanation: Their slow breeding makes populations vulnerable to losses.

charities.name: The Peregrine Fund
charities.blurb: Conserves birds of prey worldwide, including condors.

name: Marine Iguana
range: Only the rocky shores of the Galápagos Islands, Ecuador
tagline: The only lizard that feeds in the sea
lede: When Charles Darwin saw marine iguanas piled on Galápagos lava rocks, he called them 'imps of darkness'. They may look grumpy, but they're unique: the only lizards in the world that swim into the ocean to feed.
home: Marine iguanas live only on the Galápagos Islands, basking in large groups on black lava shores. Each island has its own form, differing in size and color; during breeding season some turn red and green, especially on Española Island.
life: Marine iguanas eat red and green algae growing on rocks. Smaller iguanas graze on algae exposed at low tide, while the biggest males dive into the cold sea, sometimes more than 20 metres down. Afterward, they lie on warm rocks to heat their bodies back up.
remarkable: Eating seaweed means swallowing lots of salt. Marine iguanas remove it with special glands that connect to their nostrils, and they sneeze out the salty spray, often onto their own heads, which turn white. During El Niño years, when food is scarce, they can shrink, even shortening their bones.
outlook: Marine iguanas are vulnerable. Introduced cats, dogs and rats eat eggs and young, El Niño events cause mass starvation, and oil spills and warming seas threaten their algae. Removing invasive predators from islands has been a major conservation success.
didYouKnow: Marine iguanas can hold their breath for up to an hour, though most dives are much shorter.

quiz.prompt: What do marine iguanas eat?
quiz.explanation: They feed on algae growing on rocks in and near the sea.

quiz.prompt: How do marine iguanas get rid of extra salt?
choices: They sneeze it out through their noses
They drink fresh water from streams
quiz.explanation: Salt glands connected to the nostrils let them sneeze out salt.

quiz.prompt: What can marine iguanas do when food is scarce?
choices: Shrink their bodies, even their bones
quiz.explanation: During El Niño famines they can shrink in length.

charities.name: Galápagos Conservancy
charities.blurb: Funds restoration and protection of Galápagos wildlife and islands.

name: European Hedgehog
range: Western and northern Europe, from Britain and Scandinavia to Italy; introduced to New Zealand
tagline: The garden's prickly night-time visitor
lede: For many Europeans, a snuffling hedgehog in the garden after dark is a small piece of magic. Covered in thousands of spines, it trundles across lawns and hedgerows each night, sniffing out beetles, worms and slugs.
home: European hedgehogs live in woodland edges, hedgerows, farmland, parks and gardens across western Europe. They have adapted well to towns, where gardens can be a rich hunting ground, if fences and walls don't block their way.
life: Hedgehogs are nocturnal and solitary, roaming one to 2 kilometres a night in search of beetles, caterpillars, earthworms and slugs. From about November to March, they hibernate in nests of leaves, their heart rate falling from around 190 to about 20 beats a minute.
remarkable: An adult has around 5,000 to 7,000 spines, which are hollow hairs made of keratin. When frightened, it rolls into a tight, prickly ball using a band of muscle along its back. Hedgehogs also 'self-anoint', frothing at the mouth and spreading foamy saliva over their spines, and nobody is sure why.
outlook: In 2024, the IUCN moved the European hedgehog to near threatened. Populations in Britain and several other countries have fallen sharply, due to lost hedgerows, intensive farming, roads and tidy gardens. Cutting a 13-centimetre hole in your fence creates a 'hedgehog highway'.
didYouKnow: Hedgehogs got their name because they forage in hedges and make pig-like grunts while they hunt.

quiz.prompt: About how many spines does an adult hedgehog have?
quiz.explanation: Adults carry roughly 5,000 to 7,000 spines.

quiz.prompt: What is a 'hedgehog highway'?
choices: A small hole in a garden fence so hedgehogs can pass
A trail of food left out at night
quiz.explanation: Holes about 13 cm wide let hedgehogs roam between gardens.

quiz.prompt: What do hedgehogs do in winter?
choices: Grow thicker spines and stay active
quiz.explanation: They hibernate from about November to March.

charities.name: British Hedgehog Preservation Society
charities.blurb: Runs Hedgehog Street and supports hedgehog rescue and research in the UK.

name: Komodo Dragon
range: Komodo, Rinca, Flores and a few nearby islands in Indonesia
tagline: The largest lizard on Earth
lede: Komodo dragons are real dragons, more or less. Growing up to 3 metres long, they are the largest living lizards, top predators on a handful of Indonesian islands, able to take down deer and water buffalo.
home: Komodo dragons live only on a few islands in Indonesia, including Komodo, Rinca and parts of Flores, in dry savanna and tropical forest. Komodo National Park, a World Heritage Site, was created to protect them.
life: Komodos hunt deer, wild pigs and water buffalo by ambush, and happily eat carrion. They can eat up to 80 percent of their body weight in a single meal. Young dragons spend their first years living in trees, safe from cannibalistic adults.
remarkable: A Komodo's bite is deadly partly because of venom glands in its lower jaw, which cause bleeding and shock, so even prey that escapes may die later. They flick forked tongues to 'taste' the air, finding carrion kilometres away. And females can sometimes lay fertile eggs without ever meeting a male.
outlook: Komodo dragons are endangered, with only a few thousand left. Their tiny island range is threatened by rising sea levels, habitat loss on Flores, and the hunting of their prey. Komodo National Park protects most of the remaining population.
didYouKnow: Komodo dragon teeth are coated with iron, which helps keep their serrated edges sharp.

quiz.prompt: What makes a Komodo dragon's bite so deadly?
choices: Venom from glands in its jaw
Teeth as long as a knife
quiz.explanation: Venom glands in the lower jaw cause bleeding and shock.

quiz.prompt: What can female Komodo dragons sometimes do?
choices: Lay fertile eggs without a male
quiz.explanation: This is called parthenogenesis and has been seen in zoos.

quiz.prompt: How do young Komodo dragons stay safe?
choices: They hide inside their eggs for a year
Their mothers guard them for years
quiz.explanation: Young dragons climb trees to avoid hungry adults.

charities.name: WWF
charities.blurb: Works across Indonesia to protect threatened species and island habitats.

name: Peacock Mantis Shrimp
range: Coral reefs of the Indo-Pacific, from East Africa to Guam
tagline: A rainbow with a punch like a bullet
lede: The peacock mantis shrimp looks like a living rainbow, and it hits like a heavyweight. Its club-shaped arms strike with the acceleration of a bullet, fast enough to shatter snail shells and, now and then, aquarium glass.
home: Peacock mantis shrimp live on coral reefs and sandy seafloors of the tropical Indian and Pacific oceans. They dig U-shaped burrows in rubble and sand, watching the reef from the entrance with their strange, stalked eyes.
life: They hunt crabs, snails and clams, smashing through shells with their clubs. Mantis shrimp are not true shrimp; they belong to a separate group, the stomatopods, that split from other crustaceans hundreds of millions of years ago. Some pairs stay together for years.
remarkable: The strike is so fast that it boils the water, creating a collapsing bubble that hits the prey a second time. Their eyes have 12 to 16 kinds of color receptors, compared with our three, and can see polarised and ultraviolet light, each eye moving independently.
outlook: The peacock mantis shrimp hasn't been assessed by the IUCN, and it is common on many reefs. But like all reef life, it depends on healthy coral, which is threatened by warming oceans, bleaching, pollution and destructive fishing.
didYouKnow: Engineers study the mantis shrimp's club, which can survive thousands of impacts, to design tougher materials for helmets and aircraft.

quiz.prompt: How does a peacock mantis shrimp break shells?
choices: By dropping them from a height
quiz.explanation: Its clubs strike with the acceleration of a bullet.

quiz.prompt: How many types of color receptors do its eyes have?
quiz.explanation: Mantis shrimp have far more color receptor types than we do.

quiz.prompt: What hits the prey a second time after a strike?
choices: A collapsing bubble in the boiling water
quiz.explanation: The strike creates a cavitation bubble that collapses with force.

charities.name: Oceana
charities.blurb: Campaigns to protect coral reefs and ocean habitats.

name: Common Eastern Firefly
range: Fields and lawns of eastern North America, reaching north into southern Ontario
tagline: Summer's living lanterns
lede: On warm June evenings, lawns and meadows across eastern North America start to twinkle. Those yellow-green flashes, swooping upward like a J, are male common eastern fireflies writing messages in light.
home: The common eastern firefly lives in grassy fields, meadows, parks and suburban lawns from the Great Plains to the Atlantic coast, and north into southern Ontario. It needs damp soil where its larvae can live, and darkness at night.
life: Fireflies spend most of their lives as glowing larvae in the soil, hunting snails, slugs and earthworms for one or two years. Adults live just a few weeks in summer and may barely eat. Males fly and flash; females wait in the grass and answer with a flash of their own.
remarkable: Fireflies make light with a chemical reaction between luciferin and an enzyme called luciferase. It's 'cold light': nearly all the energy becomes light, not heat. This species' signature is a rising J-shaped swoop, which earned it the nickname 'Big Dipper firefly'.
outlook: The common eastern firefly is still widespread, but many firefly species are declining. Artificial light at night drowns out their signals, pesticides harm larvae, and habitat is lost to development. Turning off outdoor lights and mowing less can bring fireflies back.
didYouKnow: The firefly enzyme luciferase is used in medical research labs to make genes and cells light up.

quiz.prompt: What shape does the male's flash trace in the air?
quiz.explanation: The J-shaped swoop earned it the nickname 'Big Dipper firefly'.

quiz.prompt: What do firefly larvae eat?
quiz.explanation: The larvae are predators in the soil.

quiz.prompt: What is a major threat to fireflies?
quiz.explanation: Light pollution drowns out the flashes they use to find mates.

charities.name: Xerces Society
charities.blurb: Leads firefly conservation research and the Firefly Atlas project.

name: Ruby-throated Hummingbird
range: Breeds across eastern North America to southern Canada; winters in Central America
tagline: A bird lighter than a coin that crosses the Gulf
lede: The ruby-throated hummingbird weighs about 3 grams, less than a Canadian quarter coin. Yet each autumn, many of them fly nonstop across the Gulf of Mexico, around 800 kilometres of open water, in a single overnight flight.
home: This is the only hummingbird that breeds in eastern North America, nesting from the Gulf states to southern Canada, as far north as Nova Scotia and the Prairies. It visits gardens, forest edges and meadows full of flowers, and spends the winter in Central America.
life: Hummingbirds drink nectar from flowers like bee balm and jewelweed, and catch tiny insects and spiders for protein. Females build walnut-sized nests of plant down bound with spider silk, which stretch as the chicks grow. They raise the young completely alone.
remarkable: Its wings beat about 50 times a second, and its heart can race over 1,000 beats a minute. To survive cold nights, it can enter torpor, a deep sleep where its body cools and its heart slows dramatically. The male's ruby throat is made by structure, not pigment, and looks black at the wrong angle.
outlook: Ruby-throated hummingbirds are common and stable. Planting native flowers that bloom across the season helps them, as does keeping feeders clean with plain sugar water, four parts water to one part sugar, with no red dye.
didYouKnow: Before migrating, a ruby-throated hummingbird can almost double its weight in fat to fuel the trip.

quiz.prompt: How do many ruby-throats reach Central America in autumn?
choices: A nonstop flight across the Gulf of Mexico
Riding on the backs of geese
Hopping island to island over months
quiz.explanation: Many fly about 800 km across the Gulf in one go.

quiz.prompt: Why can the male's red throat look black?
choices: Its color comes from structure, which depends on the angle
quiz.explanation: Iridescent structural color only flashes red at certain angles.

quiz.prompt: How do hummingbirds survive cold nights?
choices: They enter torpor, slowing their heart and cooling down
They fly all night to stay warm
quiz.explanation: Torpor saves precious energy overnight.

charities.name: Birds Canada
charities.blurb: Monitors and protects birds across Canada, from backyards to the boreal.

name: Wandering Albatross
range: The Southern Ocean, breeding on islands like South Georgia, Crozet and Kerguelen
tagline: The widest wings in the world
lede: No living bird has longer wings than the wandering albatross. Spread out, they can stretch more than 3 metres from tip to tip. With them, this great seabird glides around the Southern Ocean for months, sometimes circling the globe.
home: Wandering albatrosses spend most of their lives over the open Southern Ocean, among the strongest winds on Earth. They come ashore only to breed, on remote, windswept islands such as South Georgia, Crozet, Kerguelen and the Prince Edward Islands.
life: They feed on squid and fish, mostly snatched from the surface, often at night. Pairs mate for life and perform elaborate dances. They lay a single egg, and raising the chick takes almost a year, so most pairs breed only every two years. They don't start breeding until around ten years old.
remarkable: Albatrosses use 'dynamic soaring', swooping between faster winds above and slower air near the waves to gain energy, so they can travel huge distances while barely flapping. A wandering albatross can cover hundreds of kilometres in a day, and they can live more than 50 years.
outlook: The wandering albatross is vulnerable. Many drown after grabbing baited hooks on longline fishing boats. Simple fixes like bird-scaring lines, weighted hooks and setting lines at night dramatically reduce these deaths, and campaigns are spreading them across fleets.
didYouKnow: Albatrosses have a special shoulder lock that holds their wings out without using muscle, letting them glide for hours with little effort.

quiz.prompt: What record does the wandering albatross hold?
choices: The longest wingspan of any living bird
quiz.explanation: Its wings can span more than 3 metres.

quiz.prompt: What is the main human threat to wandering albatrosses?
choices: Baited hooks on longline fishing boats
quiz.explanation: Albatrosses drown after taking bait from longlines.

quiz.prompt: How do albatrosses travel so far without flapping?
choices: Flapping very fast in short bursts
quiz.explanation: Dynamic soaring extracts energy from changes in wind speed.

charities.name: BirdLife International
charities.blurb: Runs the Albatross Task Force, working with fishers to stop seabird bycatch.
